passages.t: ‘Now is the day of salvation’, and a servant's hardships
passages.happening:
Paul has just pleaded, ‘Be reconciled to God.’ Now he speaks to the church directly. “As God’s fellow workers, then, we urge you not to receive God’s grace in vain” (verse 1).

He quotes Isaiah: “For He says: ‘In the time of favor I heard you, and in the day of salvation I helped you.’” Then he applies it: “Behold, now is the time of favor; now is the day of salvation!” (verse 2).

Paul tries to put no stumbling block in anyone's way (verse 3). Then he shows what a servant of God looks like. It is a long list, in three movements.

First, what he has endured: “in great endurance; in troubles, hardships, and calamities; in beatings, imprisonments, and riots; in labor, sleepless nights, and hunger” (verses 4-5).

Then, what God has given him to carry it with: “in purity, knowledge, patience, and kindness; in the Holy Spirit and in sincere love; in truthful speech and in the power of God” (verses 6-7).

Last, a string of opposites, how the world sees them and what is true: “viewed as imposters, yet genuine; as unknown, yet well-known; dying, and yet we live on; punished, yet not killed; sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; poor, yet making many rich; having nothing, and yet possessing everything” (verses 8-10).
passages.hearers:
‘Receive God's grace in vain’ means to hear it and let it come to nothing, to take the gift and not let it shape your life. Paul is speaking to believers. The Corinthians had received the gospel, yet some were drifting toward a different way of thinking, one that judged by appearances. Paul warns them not to waste what they have been given.

‘The time of favor’ is a season God has opened. The Greek word for ‘time’ here, kairos, means a fitting moment, the right time, rather than time passing. Paul says that moment is now, because Christ has come.

Then the list. Corinth admired people who could show their success: fine speech, good connections, wealth, honour. Paul's rivals seem to have done just that. Paul offers a very different kind of proof. Beatings. Prison. Riots. Hunger. Sleepless nights. This is not a list anyone in Corinth would boast of. Paul puts it first.

Acts tells some of it. Paul and Silas were beaten and thrown into prison at Philippi (Acts 16:22-24). There was a riot at Ephesus (Acts 19:23-41). Paul worked with his own hands to support himself (1 Thessalonians 2:9). He will give a longer list in chapter 11.

The last part of the list sets two views side by side. To the world, Paul looked like a fraud, a nobody, a dying man, a sad and poor man with nothing. The truth was the other side of each pair. And notice ‘poor, yet making many rich’. That is the pattern of Christ himself, who “though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor” (8:9).
passages.ot:
Paul quotes Isaiah 49:8. In the BSB, which follows the Hebrew, God says to his servant, “In the time of favor I will answer You, and in the day of salvation I will help You” (Isaiah 49:8). Paul's wording, ‘I heard you’ and ‘I helped you’, differs a little. He may be following the old Greek translation of Isaiah used in his day. The meaning is the same: God has set a time to save.

The verse comes just after one of Isaiah's songs about God's servant, where God says, “I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). Christians read those songs as fulfilled in Jesus. Paul now says the time of favor promised to the servant has come for everyone who hears.

The prophets also called people to seek God in his time: “Seek the LORD while He may be found; call on Him while He is near” (Isaiah 55:6). And a psalm says, “Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts” (Psalm 95:7-8).

Paul's ‘dying, and yet we live on’ echoes the psalm he quotes in Romans: “Yet for Your sake we face death all day long; we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered” (Psalm 44:22).
passages.hard:
Is ‘now is the day of salvation’ meant to pressure people into a quick decision?

Paul is urgent, and he means it. But look at whom he is speaking to and why. He is speaking to believers in Corinth, and his urgency comes from what God has done: the time of favor has arrived in Christ. It is good news first, an open door. Paul is not using fear or tricks to push anyone. In the very next breath he lists his own sufferings, and says his aim is to put “no obstacle in anyone’s way” (verse 3).

So the verse is an invitation, not a threat. God's door is open now. No one reading it needs to feel cornered. It asks only that God's grace not be received in vain.
passages.asks: Paul lists hardships and virtues side by side. Ask which of the virtues in verses 6 and 7 you most need God to grow in you: patience, kindness, sincere love, truthful speech. Then look at the opposites of verses 8 to 10. Where does the world's view of a faithful life differ from God's? And what would it mean for you not to receive God's grace in vain?

passages.happening:
Now Paul speaks to them by name. “We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians. Our hearts are open wide” (verse 11).

The problem is not on his side. “It is not our affection, but yours, that is restrained” (verse 12).

So he asks them for the same. “As a fair exchange, I ask you as my children: Open wide your hearts also” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Paul seldom calls a church by its name in the middle of a letter. When he does, it is a moment of strong feeling. Here he has just poured out his life before them, and he speaks to them directly: ‘Corinthians’.

In Greek, ‘We have spoken freely’ is, word for word, ‘our mouth has been opened to you’. And ‘our hearts are open wide’ is ‘our heart has been made wide’. Paul has held nothing back. There is room in his heart for all of them.

Then ‘restrained’. The word means pressed into a narrow space, cramped. The Corinthians have made their hearts small toward him. Perhaps they had listened to his critics. Perhaps they still held some hurt from the painful visit.

‘As my children.’ Paul had told them before, “in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel” (1 Corinthians 4:15). A father who has been pushed away asks his children to let him back in. He does not order it. He asks for ‘a fair exchange’: open hearts on both sides.
passages.ot:
The picture of an enlarged heart is in the Psalms. “I run in the path of Your commandments, for You will enlarge my heart” (Psalm 119:32). There it is God who makes the heart wide.

Isaiah pictures a heart that swells with joy when God brings his scattered people home: “your heart will tremble and swell with joy” (Isaiah 60:5).

And Paul's appeal as a father echoes the way the Scriptures speak of God himself, pleading with his children to come back. Through Jeremiah God says, “Return, O faithless children, and I will heal your faithlessness” (Jeremiah 3:22).
passages.asks: Paul's heart was open wide, and the Corinthians' hearts were cramped. Ask whether there is someone you have closed your heart to, perhaps for a good reason, perhaps not. Ask what it would take to make room again. And ask whether there is someone whose love you have held at arm's length, who is asking you, as Paul did, for a fair exchange.

passages.happening:
Paul gives a sharp warning. “Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership can righteousness have with wickedness? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness?” (verse 14).

More questions follow, each pairing two things that cannot go together. “What harmony is there between Christ and Belial? Or what does a believer have in common with an unbeliever?” (verse 15). “What agreement can exist between the temple of God and idols? For we are the temple of the living God” (verse 16).

Then Paul gives a chain of God's promises from the Scriptures. God will live among them and be their God (verse 16). So they must come out and be separate, and touch nothing unclean, and God will receive them (verse 17). “And: ‘I will be a Father to you, and you will be My sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty’” (verse 18).

The thought ends in the next chapter: “Therefore, beloved, since we have these promises, let us cleanse ourselves from everything that defiles body and spirit” (7:1).
passages.hearers:
A yoke is a wooden bar that joins two animals so they can pull a plough or a cart together. If one is an ox and the other a donkey, they cannot pull as one. They differ in size, strength and pace. The law of Moses forbade yoking them together.

Paul uses the picture for a bond between a believer and unbelief that pulls the believer away from Christ. What did he have in view in Corinth? Look at his examples: light and darkness, Christ and Belial, the temple of God and idols. Corinth was full of temples. Much of its social life, trade guild dinners, family feasts, civic festivals, took place in temple dining rooms, with food offered to the city's gods. In his first letter Paul had warned the church not to take part in the worship of idols: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons too” (1 Corinthians 10:21). Most readers think that is the main concern here too: partnership in idolatry, and ties that would draw believers back into it.

‘Belial’ comes from a Hebrew word meaning worthlessness. In the Old Testament it is used for wicked men. By Paul's day some Jewish writings used it as a name for Satan. Paul's Greek spells it ‘Beliar’. It appears only here in the New Testament, as does the Greek word for ‘unequally yoked’.

‘We are the temple of the living God.’ Paul means the church together. In a city of temples, he says the place where God truly lives is a gathering of ordinary believers. That is why it must not be mixed with the worship of idols.
passages.ot:
The picture comes from the law: “Do not plow with an ox and a donkey yoked together” (Deuteronomy 22:10). The same law forbade mixing two kinds of seed or cloth (Leviticus 19:19). And a psalm uses the very word ‘yoke’ for Israel's idolatry: “They yoked themselves to Baal of Peor and ate sacrifices offered to lifeless gods” (Psalm 106:28).

Then comes a chain of quotations, woven together. Paul names no book, but each line can be traced.

‘I will dwell with them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be My people’ joins two promises. The first is from the law: “I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people” (Leviticus 26:12). The second is from Ezekiel: “My dwelling place will be with them; I will be their God, and they will be My people” (Ezekiel 37:27).

‘Come out from among them and be separate’ and ‘Touch no unclean thing’ are from Isaiah, who called God's people to leave Babylon: “Depart, depart, go out from there! Touch no unclean thing” (Isaiah 52:11).

‘I will receive you’ is close to Ezekiel's promise to gather the scattered people: “I will accept you as a pleasing aroma” (Ezekiel 20:41).

‘I will be a Father to you, and you will be My sons’ comes from God's promise about David's son: “I will be his Father, and he will be My son” (2 Samuel 7:14). Paul widens it to all God's people and adds ‘daughters’, as Isaiah does: “Bring My sons from afar, and My daughters from the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 43:6). ‘The Lord Almighty’ matches the title in 2 Samuel 7:8, which the BSB, from the Hebrew, gives as ‘the LORD of Hosts’.
passages.hard:
‘Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers.’ Does this mean a believer should leave a husband or wife who does not believe, or keep away from people who do not share their faith?

No, to both. Paul himself says so in his first letter to the same church. To a believer already married to an unbeliever, he writes, “If a brother has an unbelieving wife and she is willing to live with him, he must not divorce her” (1 Corinthians 7:12). The same is true for a believing wife (1 Corinthians 7:13). So no one should take this verse as a reason to leave a spouse. If you are married to someone who does not share your faith, Paul's word to you is to stay, if they are willing, and to live in peace. Nothing here, or in 1 Corinthians 7, asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger; the site's note on 1 Corinthians 7:10-16 says more, and the Find Help page lists places to turn.

Nor is this a call to withdraw from the world. Paul had already corrected that mistake. He told the Corinthians that keeping away from every sinner in the city was not what he meant, “In that case you would have to leave this world” (1 Corinthians 5:10). Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners. Believers are to be friends, neighbours, coworkers and good citizens with people of every faith and none. Nothing here gives anyone a reason to look down on unbelievers.

What, then, does it mean? Most readers think Paul's first concern was sharing in idol worship, and any tie that would draw believers back into it. How far it reaches beyond that, Christians answer differently. Many churches teach from this verse that a believer should marry only a believer. They set it beside Paul's word that a widow may marry again, “as long as he belongs to the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39). Some apply it to business partnerships, to joining organizations whose aims conflict with Christ, or to shared religious worship. Others think it should be kept closer to its first setting, and warn against making it a rule for every friendship or business deal. These notes do not choose. All agree on the heart of it: a believer should not enter a bond that requires them to split their loyalty to Christ.

Some scholars think these verses were brought here from another letter, because 6:13 seems to run straight on to 7:2; others read them as Paul's own, set here on purpose, and the book page sets out both views.
passages.asks: Paul says the church is the temple of the living God. Ask whether anything in your life is pulling you away from Christ, a partnership, a habit, a loyalty you would not want to name. Then ask the other question too: are there people outside the church whom you have kept at a distance, when Jesus would have sat down to eat with them?
